messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sameer, a 41-year-old architect, presented as a man holding himself together with immense effort, his posture rigid and his gaze constantly scanning the room. The trauma occurred eight months prior, but for Sameer, it was a continuous present. The event itself was a brutal culmination of a relationship that had become quietly volatile. His then-partner, Mark, had come home drunk, the smell of whiskey sharp and cloying in their apartment. An argument, fueled by alcohol, had escalated with terrifying speed. Mark’s words slurred into an incomprehensible roar of accusation, and then the violence began. Sameer remembers the attack not as a fluid sequence but as a series of stark, still images, like a slideshow from a nightmare. He sees the glint of the lamp, a fist, the pattern of the rug rushing toward his face. He remembers the feeling of being too sick and dizzy to get up, the world a blur of noise and pain.

In the months that followed, Sameer found that the world had been wired with triggers connected directly to that night. The smell of alcohol is the most potent; at a recent firm reception, a colleague opened a bottle of scotch nearby, and the scent instantly plunged him back into the memory. He saw not his colleague but Mark’s face, contorted with rage, and his body reacted before his mind could catch up. A wave of terror washed over him, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape, a physical certainty of imminent danger that was utterly disconnected from the safe reality of the reception. This happens constantly; his body is a sentry that has long since abandoned its post in the present, reacting to threats that only it can see.

This state of constant threat has become his new baseline, a high-frequency hum of anxiety that makes ordinary life feel treacherous. He is jumpy, startling violently at the sound of a dropped book or a car backfiring. At his open-plan office, the overlapping conversations of his colleagues often merge into a meaningless, threatening chatter. This auditory chaos doesn't just distract him; it yanks him back to the memory of Mark’s incoherent shouting. The memory, in turn, amplifies his sense of threat, leaving him drenched in the same cold terror he felt on the floor of his old apartment. Because he is always anticipating an attack, his mind is primed to find these echoes everywhere, turning the ambient noise of his workplace into a personal torment. Feeling so perpetually endangered has become its own kind of evidence for him; it has quietly confirmed the crushing belief that he is no longer a person who can function in the world, that he failed so badly he has become permanently fragile. This perpetual state of vigilance makes the intrusive, photographic stills of the assault more frequent and vivid, as if his mind is constantly re-opening the wound to check if it’s still there.

The memories themselves are a source of profound distress. When the snapshots flash into his mind—the raised hand, the shattered glass—they are not just images but full-bodied re-experiences. The terror is immediate and absolute, and it invariably brings with it a cascade of self-recrimination. He sees his own inaction in those frozen moments and is consumed by the belief that he failed. He was betrayed by the person he trusted most, and the memory of that betrayal is inextricably linked to the conviction that he should have seen it coming, should have done something different. This appraisal—that he can’t trust his own judgment—has poisoned his self-concept. The memory of being helpless fuels the present-day belief that he is fundamentally incapable of doing the right thing to protect himself.

This corrosive self-doubt has become the engine of his hypervigilance. The world feels profoundly unsafe to Sameer precisely because he has come to believe he is inadequate to navigate it. The conviction that he failed in his most important role—to keep himself safe—means he cannot trust his own instincts. This forces his body to remain on high alert, a desperate compensation for a mind he no longer trusts. Sleep offers no respite; he lies awake for hours, convinced that he must stay alert for a danger he cannot name but feels in his bones. Even a simple head cold can become a trigger; the feeling of physical unwellness is a direct echo of his helplessness during the assault, and with it comes the crushing thought that he is weak, a failure.

His life has shrunk dramatically. He and his wife, Priya, now sleep in separate rooms because of his inability to rest. He feels he is failing her, a ghost in his own marriage. He finally sought therapy after an incident last week. Priya had tried to comfort him after a loud noise made him cry out, and he flinched away from her touch so violently that she recoiled, her face a mask of hurt. It was in that moment, seeing the pain he was causing the person he loved most, that he realised the trauma was not just living inside him, but was actively destroying the life he had tried so hard to build.
